adults.title: The Quiet Courage of a Disciple
adults.big_idea: Faith in Jesus Christ gives us courage to choose the right, and each courageous choice makes that faith stronger.
adults.objective: Learners will name one place in their own discipleship that calls for spiritual courage right now and choose one act of faith in Christ to meet it this week.
prepare: Read Elder Andersen's talk, marking paragraphs T21.05, T21.11, T21.13–T21.24.
Bring paper and pens for silent writing.
Draw a large circle on the board with two words on it, one at the top and one at the bottom: Faith in Christ, Courage. Leave the arrows off for now.
Be ready to read aloud the short account of the Woodbury family (T21.18).

segments.name: Courage no one saw
steps: Begin with prayer. Then say that Elder Andersen taught that faith and courage are hallmarks of disciples of Jesus Christ.
Ask learners to think silently for thirty seconds about the first question below.
Invite them to turn to a neighbor and share only as much as they wish. Take two or three brief responses from the room.
questions: When has doing the right thing taken more courage than anyone around you realized?
Where did the strength to do it come from?

segments.name: What spiritual courage is
steps: Have someone read Elder Andersen's definition from T21.05 (see key quotes). Ask which of the three, obstacles, doubt or fear, feels most real to people today, and why.

Read T21.11 aloud slowly. Invite a learner to come to the board and draw the arrows on the circle to show what Elder Andersen described: faith in Christ brings courage, and courage to choose the right strengthens faith.
Read Moroni 1:3 together. Point out that Elder Andersen said our world is different from Moroni's day, but discipleship always requires courage.
questions: Why do you think the Lord lets faith and courage grow together, each feeding the other?

segments.name: Courage in ordinary discipleship
steps: Divide into groups of three or four. Assign each group two or three of these paragraphs: T21.13 (private prayer), T21.14 (the sacrament), T21.15–T21.16 (accepting a calling; President Oaks), T21.17 (commandments and unforeseen trouble), T21.19–T21.20 (young people; a young mother on Sunday morning), T21.21 (speaking of the Savior, covenants, repentance, following prophets).
Ask each group to read their paragraphs and talk about the questions below. Give them five minutes.
Invite one sentence from each group: the kind of courage in their paragraphs that they most admire in someone they know. No names are needed.
questions: Which of these takes real courage for people in our ward or family right now?
In your paragraphs, what does the Lord give in return for the courage?

segments.name: When life is upended
steps: Read aloud the account of Cody and Haylee Woodbury in T21.18. Then summarize gently, without adding detail, the woman in T21.22 who bore testimony that in happiness or unspeakable grief she would trust her Savior.
Read 2 Corinthians 4:8 together. Ask learners to notice what Paul says after each trouble.
Share Sister Runia's words from this conference (see aligned quotes) and ask the question below. Allow silence before anyone answers.
questions: What is the difference between faith that expects to be spared the storm and faith that stands on the rock during it?

segments.name: Stillness
steps: Retell briefly Elder Andersen's summers on the dairy farm: guiding the cows to a high meadow and spending the day alone with his thoughts, with no phone and no music. Read his conclusion: “We need stillness to nourish our faith in Christ.”
Read the line from President David O. McKay that Elder Andersen heard as a young man (see aligned quotes).
Hand out paper. Give two minutes of real silence for learners to write an answer to the question below. No one will be asked to share.
questions: What battle is being fought in the silent chambers of my soul, and when this week will I be still enough to kneel alone and speak with Heavenly Father about it?

segments.name: Choose and trust the promise
steps: Read Elder Andersen's promise in T21.24 (see key quotes). Ask learners to listen for the three blessings he promised. Check understanding by having the class name them: answers will come, spiritual power will increase, and courage in following Christ will define the eternal soul.
Read John 14:23, which Elder Andersen quoted, and ask what the Savior promises those who love Him and keep His words.
Invite each learner to write one specific act of courage for this week beneath what they wrote earlier. Offer the ideas in the act list if helpful.
Bear your witness of the Savior. Tell the class that next week you will begin by asking two or three people what they noticed about their faith after they acted.

key_quotes.text: Spiritual courage is the triumph over obstacles, doubt, and fear in choosing the right.

As we choose faith in Christ, He blesses us with the courage, sometimes in very difficult situations, to choose the right, and as we manifest our courage to choose the right, our faith in Christ strengthens.
In those quiet moments when we speak with our Heavenly Father privately, independently, we are given the increased courage to choose the right.

I promise you that as you strengthen your faith in Jesus Christ by believing and following Him and keeping His commandments, your answers will come, your spiritual power will increase, and your courage in following Christ will define your eternal soul.

scriptures.use: Read together in the second segment as an example of courage born of faith in Christ when a disciple stands alone.
Read together in the fourth segment; have learners notice what Paul says follows each trouble for those whose hope is in Christ.
Read in the closing segment; ask what the Savior promises those who love Him and keep His words.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President David O. McKay
aligned_quotes.text: The greatest battle of life is fought within the silent chambers of your own soul.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Sister Runia
aligned_quotes.text: The gospel isn’t the umbrella; it’s the solid rock we’re standing on during the storm

takeaways: Spiritual courage is choosing the right in spite of obstacles, doubt and fear.
Faith in Christ brings courage, and acting with courage strengthens faith.
Quiet, private prayer is where the Lord gives increased courage.
act: Set aside one period of real stillness this week, with the phone in another room, to kneel alone and pray about the battle you wrote down.
Do the one act of courage you chose, and afterward write a sentence about what happened to your faith.
During the sacrament, think about one covenant you will need courage to keep this week.
Tell someone whose quiet courage you admire what you have seen in them.
adapt: At home with two or three adults: skip the groups and read T21.13–T21.21 aloud in turns, pausing whenever someone says, That one is me.
Large class: keep people in pairs with those beside them instead of forming groups, and take only three reports.
Short on time: keep the definition, the stillness writing and the promise; summarize the group reading in two minutes.

youth.title: Brave Enough to Believe
youth.big_idea: When we choose faith in Jesus Christ, He gives us courage to choose the right, and using that courage makes our faith stronger.
youth.objective: Youth will explain in their own words how faith and courage strengthen each other and will commit to one specific act of spiritual courage and one time of stillness this week.
prepare: Read Elder Andersen's talk and have it open on your phone; ask youth to bring scriptures or phones.
Write on the board: Spiritual courage is the triumph over ____, ____, and ____ in choosing the right.
Bring paper strips or sticky notes and pens.
Have a timer ready (a phone works).

segments.name: Which takes more courage?
steps: As soon as the prayer ends, have everyone stand. Name one side of the room A and the other B.

Read each pair and have youth walk to the side they think takes more courage. Ask one person on each side why. Keep it quick. Pair 1: A, getting up before sunrise for seminary, or B, saying you believe in Jesus Christ when a friend asks. Pair 2: A, admitting you were wrong and repenting, or B, saying yes to a calling when you feel inadequate. Pair 3: A, praying alone when no one would know if you skipped it, or B, keeping a standard when everyone around you is not.
Tell them every one of these comes from a talk Elder Andersen gave at general conference about courage born of faith in Jesus Christ.

segments.name: Fill in the blanks
steps: Have youth open the talk on their phones and race to find the three missing words on the board (T21.05: obstacles, doubt, fear). The first to find them fills in the blanks.

Give each person three paper strips. Ask them to write, without names, one obstacle, one doubt and one fear that can make it hard for someone their age to follow the Savior. Collect them and read several aloud without comment.
Say that these are real, and that Elder Andersen said being the Savior's true disciple is not a casual pursuit.
questions: Why do you think choosing the right takes courage and not just knowing what is right?

segments.name: Three stories, six words
steps: Form three groups. Group 1: Rosemary in Zimbabwe (T21.01–T21.02). Group 2: Moroni (T21.06–T21.07 with Moroni 1:3). Group 3: Peter and John (T21.26–T21.27 with Acts 4:8–10).
Give three minutes on the timer. Each group reads its story and prepares two things: an answer to the questions below and a headline for the story of exactly six words.
Each group reports in under a minute. Let the class vote for the best headline other than their own.
Point out what the stories share: a seventeen-year-old, a man with no friends left, and two Apostles facing rulers all acted from faith in Jesus Christ.
questions: What was standing against this person?
Where did the courage come from?

segments.name: The loop
steps: Have someone read T21.11 aloud (see key quotes). Ask a volunteer to draw it on the board as a loop: faith in Christ, courage, choosing the right, stronger faith.

Tell the account of President Oaks as a young attorney working evenings and Saturdays when his stake president called him to serve in the stake mission presidency, which would take three to four evenings a week. Read what he said (see aligned quotes). Ask where his decision fits on the loop.
In pairs, have youth answer the question below, then hear from two pairs.
questions: When have you done something right that was hard, and noticed afterward that you believed more, not less?

segments.name: Just me and the cows
steps: Retell Elder Andersen's summers on the dairy farm: after milking he saddled his horse and guided three dozen cows to a high meadow, and spent the whole day with no cell phone, no earbuds, no music and no texting, alone with his thoughts. Read his words about stillness from T21.10 (see key quotes).

Try it. Ask everyone to silence phones and place them face down under their chairs. Set the timer for two minutes of complete quiet. Ask them to think about one battle they are facing and to say a silent prayer about it.
After the silence, read President McKay's words (see aligned quotes). Read from T21.13 that when we speak with Heavenly Father privately we are given increased courage to choose the right.
Ask the question below and take a few honest answers.
questions: What was that two minutes like? What makes stillness hard to find, and what could you change to get some every day?

segments.name: One brave thing
steps: Read Elder Andersen's promise in T21.24 (see key quotes). Have youth name the three things he promised.
Check understanding: ask two volunteers to explain the loop on the board in one sentence each, as if to a younger brother or sister.

Give each person a fresh strip. Have them write one brave thing they will do this week because they believe in Jesus Christ, and one daily time they will be still, with the phone away. They keep the strip in their scriptures or phone case.
Share your witness that the Savior lives and gives courage. Tell them that next week you will start by asking who did their brave thing and what happened to their faith.

key_quotes.text: Spiritual courage is the triumph over obstacles, doubt, and fear in choosing the right.

As we choose faith in Christ, He blesses us with the courage, sometimes in very difficult situations, to choose the right, and as we manifest our courage to choose the right, our faith in Christ strengthens.
Times have changed, but our spirits have not changed. We need stillness to nourish our faith in Christ.

I promise you that as you strengthen your faith in Jesus Christ by believing and following Him and keeping His commandments, your answers will come, your spiritual power will increase, and your courage in following Christ will define your eternal soul.

scriptures.use: Group 2 reads it with T21.06–T21.07 and reports what stood against Moroni and where his courage came from.
Group 3 reads it with T21.26–T21.27 and reports how Peter and John answered the rulers and in whose name.
Optional in the second segment: read it and ask how Paul's description matches the doubts, distractions and deceptions of our day.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Dallin H. Oaks
aligned_quotes.text: Gathering all my faith, I accepted the call.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President David O. McKay
aligned_quotes.text: The greatest battle of life is fought within the silent chambers of your own soul.

takeaways: Faith in Jesus Christ is where spiritual courage comes from.
Every time I choose the right when it is hard, my faith gets stronger.
I need stillness and private prayer to hear the Lord and find courage.
act: Do the one brave thing you wrote on your strip, and notice what happens to your faith.
Take ten minutes of stillness each day with your phone in another room, and use part of it to kneel and pray alone.
If a friend asks what you believe this week, answer honestly in one sentence about the Savior.
During the sacrament on Sunday, think about one promise you will need courage to keep at school.
adapt: Fewer than six youth: do the three stories as a whole class, one at a time, and write the six-word headlines together.
At home: do the room-sides game at the kitchen table with thumbs left or right, then go straight to the two minutes of stillness and the brave-thing strip.
Short on time: keep the opening game, the loop and the two minutes of stillness; drop the headline vote.

children.title: Jesus Helps Me Be Brave
children.big_idea: Because I have faith in Jesus Christ, I can be brave and choose the right.
children.objective: Children will say that Jesus helps them be brave and will draw one brave, right choice they can make this week.
prepare: Read Elder Andersen's talk, especially T21.02, T21.06–T21.07 and T21.10–T21.13.
Bring building blocks (or small boxes or paper cups to stack).
Bring paper and crayons for each child.
Fold one sheet of paper in half like a small booklet for the first story.

segments.name: Stand tall
steps: After the prayer, ask the children to curl up small like someone who feels afraid. Then ask them to stand tall like someone who is brave.

Teach the truth for today with actions: “Jesus” (point up), “helps me” (hands on heart), “be brave” (stand tall, arms strong). Say it together three times, a little louder each time, then once in a whisper.
Tell them that at general conference Elder Andersen, an Apostle of Jesus Christ, taught that faith in Jesus helps us be brave to choose the right.

segments.name: Rosemary and the little book
steps: Hold up the folded paper. Tell the story simply: Rosemary was seventeen and lived in a country called Zimbabwe. Missionaries left a pamphlet about Joseph Smith at her home. She read it and felt right away that it was true. Joseph really did see Heavenly Father and Jesus Christ. She was taught and was baptized.
Act it out. Choose a child to be Rosemary, who finds the pamphlet, reads it and puts a hand on her heart. The others are missionaries who teach her. Repeat with a new Rosemary if time allows.
Explain that Rosemary chose to follow Jesus, and she was a good example to her mother and father, who joined the Church many years later.
Say the truth with actions again.
questions: How do you think Rosemary felt inside when she knew it was true?
What brave thing did Rosemary choose to do?

segments.name: Moroni would not say no to Jesus
steps: Tell the children that Moroni lived long ago and wrote in the Book of Mormon. He was all alone. He had no friends and nowhere to go. People around him wanted him to say he did not believe in Jesus.
Read Moroni's words from the talk: “And I, Moroni, will not deny the Christ.” Explain that deny means to say I do not believe.

Play Stand for Jesus. The children sit. Each time you say something a follower of Jesus would do (pray, tell the truth, be kind to someone left out, say sorry), they jump up and stand tall. For anything else (push in line, tell a lie), they stay sitting and shake their heads.
Ask the question below.
questions: Who helped Moroni be brave when he was all alone?

segments.name: The quiet meadow
steps: Tell the children that when Elder Andersen was a boy he lived on a small dairy farm. On summer mornings after milking he got on his horse and took the cows up to a high meadow to eat grass.
Let the children be cows walking slowly around the room while you lead on a pretend horse. Then say: Now we are in the meadow. Everyone sit down. It is very quiet here.

Sit in silence together for thirty seconds. Whisper that Elder Andersen spent the whole day there with his thoughts, and he taught: “We need stillness to nourish our faith in Christ.” Explain that nourish means to feed and help grow.

Teach that when we are still and pray to Heavenly Father by ourselves, He helps us be brave to choose the right. Have the children fold their arms and think quietly for a moment about Heavenly Father.
questions: When is a quiet time that you can pray?

segments.name: Building my faith
steps: Set the blocks in the middle. Put down the first block and say: This is my faith in Jesus Christ.

Give a simple pretend situation, such as: A boy sees someone sitting alone at recess. What is the brave, right choice? When a child answers, that child adds a block. Other situations: a girl broke something and no one saw; friends are saying unkind words; it is time to pray and a boy feels shy; a new child comes to Primary.
As the tower grows, explain what Elder Andersen taught: when we are brave and choose the right, our faith in Jesus grows stronger. If the tower falls, smile and build again; we can always try again.
Share President Oaks's words from the talk (see aligned quotes). Explain that he was once asked to do something that felt very big, and he used all his faith and said yes.
questions: What happened to our tower each time someone chose the right?

segments.name: My brave choice
steps: Give each child paper and crayons. Ask them to draw themselves making one brave, right choice this week.
Walk around and ask each child to tell you about the drawing. Help write a few words on it if they wish.
Sing “Choose the Right Way” quietly while they finish, if the children know it.

segments.name: Show and say
steps: Invite two or three children to show their drawings and tell their brave choice.
Say the truth with actions one last time. Bear a simple testimony that Jesus Christ lives and helps you be brave.
Ask the children to take the drawing home and put it where they will see it. Tell them that next week you will ask them to tell about their brave choice.

key_quotes.text: Faith and courage are hallmarks of disciples of Jesus Christ.
And I, Moroni, will not deny the Christ.
We need stillness to nourish our faith in Christ.

scriptures.use: Show the children where Moroni's words are in the Book of Mormon; an older child can read the verse aloud during the Moroni segment.
For older children: read it at the end and ask what Jesus promises those who love Him and keep His words.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Dallin H. Oaks
aligned_quotes.text: Gathering all my faith, I accepted the call.

takeaways: I can choose the right even when it is hard.
When I am quiet and pray, Heavenly Father helps me.
act: Make the brave choice you drew, and tell a grown-up about it.
Find one quiet moment each day to pray to Heavenly Father by yourself.
Say the words and do the actions for Jesus helps me be brave when you feel afraid.

adapt.younger: For ages 3–7: keep each story to three or four sentences and act everything out. Repeat the action truth after every segment. Let every child be a cow and add a block, with a helper guiding hands. Shorten the meadow silence to ten or fifteen seconds and make the drawing a simple picture of the child standing tall.
adapt.older: For ages 8–11: have a child read Moroni 1:3 aloud and another read the sentence about Rosemary from the talk. Let an older child lead the Stand for Jesus game and make up the block situations. Ask a harder question: Why does choosing the right when it is hard make faith stronger? Have them write one sentence under their drawing about when and where they will make their brave choice.
